paper_title: Distilling Visual Agents from Limited Interaction Experience

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: How much interaction experience is needed to distill a capable visual agent? We study learning from few tasks and recorded interaction histories. Our framework selects representative trajectories using skill-context coverage and ordered visual-decision similarity. On-policy distillation (OPD) learns through fresh interaction on selected tasks or fresh student responses at fixed histories. Across Navigation, Sokoban, and spatial mapping, even one online training task supports transfer to other tasks. Four fixed trajectories raise a 4B student's success from 49.17% to 82.08% on standard Navigation and from 60.16% to 85.55% on Sokoban, recovering over 90% of the measured gap to a 27B teacher on these panels. On an independent Navigation panel, replay improves success from 45.83% to 76.67%, retaining 91.36% of the same-task online gain without new interaction during optimization. Training repetitions, matched supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a 9B extension further support the value of compact experience.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: 1. Introduction How much interaction experience is needed to distill capable visual agent? We study learning from few tasks and recorded interaction histories. Our framework selects representative trajectories using skillcontext coverage and ordered visual-decision similarity. On-policy distillation (OPD) learns through fresh interaction on selected tasks or fresh student responses at ﬁxed histories. Across Navigation, Sokoban, and spatial mapping, even one online training task supports transfer to other tasks. Four ﬁxed trajectories raise 4B students success from 49.17% to 82.08% on standard Navigation and from 60.16% to 85.55% on Sokoban, recovering over 90% of the measured gap to 27B teacher on these panels. On an independent Navigation panel, replay improves success from 45.83% to 76.67%, retaining 91.36% of the same-task online gain without new interaction during optimization. Training repetitions, matched supervised ﬁne-tuning (SFT), and 9B extension further support the value of compact experience. Visual agents interpret images and feedback to complete multi-step tasks [27, 34]. Distillation transfers strong teachers behavior to smaller agent [1, 19]. We ask: how much distinct interaction experience is needed for effective transfer beyond the training experiences? Few-example learning has yielded strong gains in language-model alignment and reasoning [4, 28, 36]. Visual agents introduce sequential challenge: changed action alters subsequent observations [18]. Must distillation span many different tasks? Can few recorded histories also support transfer? We study few-task online training alongside ﬁxed-history replay. Both generate fresh student responses, but only online training executes them for new observations. Our framework selects experience from training-only pool of student trajectories. An annotation model builds skillcontext inventory and describes visual decisions from screenshots, observations, and preceding actions. coverage-ﬁrst selector combines these annotations with ordered decision similarity to choose complete trajectories. Annotations never enter student or distillation-teacher prompts. Selected tasks support online OPD; selected causal histories support preﬁx replay [11] and matched teacher-response SFT. Across three environments, even one online task supports transfer. Four ﬁxed trajectories recover over 90% of 4B students measured teacher gap on the original standard Navigation and Sokoban panels. Independent Navigation evaluation retains 91.36% of the same-task online gain. Training repetitions, matched SFT, and 9B extension further support the value of selected histories across runs, objectives, and student scales. Our contributions are: (1) evidence of visual-agent transfer from few tasks and ﬁxed histories through online and replay studies; (2) representative selection combining skill context coverage with ordered visual decisions while preserving original causal inputs; and (3) evaluation across three environments and two student scales, covering data requirements, measured teacher-gap recovery, and behavioral transfer, with selection controls, matched SFT, fullpool, and online comparisons. 2. Related Work Our study connects on-policy distillation [1, 5], preﬁx replay [11], and few-example adaptation [4, 28, 36]. We investigate whether few representative experiences support visual-agent transfer under the state-distribution shift induced by the learners actions [18]. We study representative-subset selection [15, 22, 31] at the level of complete trajectories, combining skillcontext coverage with ordered visual decision similarity. Skills and experience have also supported retrieval and planning [26, 35]; here, annotations select histories rather than augment policy prompts. Detailed comparisons with these methods, world alignment, and visual-agent training appear in the supplementary material. 3. Method 3.1. Spatial transfer spans multiple behaviors. K4 OPD improves two-room exploration coverage from 0.413 to 0.806, direction from 0.012 to 0.078, facing from 0.032 to 0.156, and position from 0.042 to 0.233. Gains span exploration and map construction; full-pool OPD improves these components further. Detailed components, uncertainty, and exposure analyses appear in the supplement. 5. Discussion Results across OPD, SFT, and student scales suggest that compact decision experience transfers beyond training tasks. Coverage and repeated supervision may help explain 8 this reuse. Scope and limitations. Small data counts distinct tasks or histories; collection and annotation remain necessary. Core results use single training runs and development-inspected panels; additional Navigation repetitions and independent evaluation broaden the evidence. 6. Conclusion Limited interaction experience supports visual-agent transfer through both few-task online OPD and ﬁxed-history replay. Four trajectories recover over 90% of the 4B teacher gap on the original standard Navigation and Sokoban panels.

sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: A. Extended Related Work Distillation and sequential distribution shift. Knowledge distillation transfers teacher predictions [6], and policy distillation transfers visual control policies [19]. Sequencelevel KD learns teacher-generated targets [7]; GKD [1], MiniLLM [5], and DistiLLM [9] study student-generated sequences and teacher feedback. DAgger [18] highlights action-induced state distribution shift. ReOPD [11] replays teacher histories with step-decaying preﬁx sampling. WAM-OPD [13] distills robotic action models through preﬁx-weighted replay of ﬁxed trajectories. We select initial-student visual histories for uniform trajectory/turn replay and compare them with few-task online interaction, examining task breadth and history refresh at matched update/response budgets. Adaptation with very little data. LIMA studies smalldata supervised alignment [36]; one-example RLVR [28] and OPD [4] show few-query reasoning gains. AdaptAgent [24] adapts multimodal web agents from few human demonstrations through in-context learning or meta-learned parameter adaptation. We study teacher-supervised visualagent transfer from selected histories and restricted task catalogues, with OPD, matched SFT, and full-pool comparisons. Few tasks or histories still require repeated response generation; replay also requires initial collection. Representative data selection. Core-set selection covers visual feature space [22], while CRAIG selects weighted subsets to approximate training gradients [15]. For language models, DSIR matches target distributions [32], DEITA combines complexity, quality, and diversity [14], and LESS uses gradient inﬂuence for targeted tuning [31]. Submodular summarization similarly balances coverage and diversity [12]. We select whole trajectories using skill context opportunities and ordered decision-description similarity. Our lexicographic rule does not directly inherit classical cardinality-constrained greedy guarantees [16]. Skills, world alignment, and visual agents. Voyager stores executable skills [26], ExpeL retrieves experiential insights [35], and WALL-EVE learns symbolic rules from trajectoryprediction conﬂicts to align world model for planning without policy training [37]. EMMA transfers reﬂection-improved actions from parallel text-world LLM to visual agent through DAgger-DPO [33]. GTR counters thought collapse during VLM RL through automated reasoning correction [30]; RAGEN [29] and GiGPO [3] study multi-turn agent RL, while VAGEN focuses on visual world-model reasoning [27]. Our annotations instead select ﬁxed histories for policy adaptation; neither learner nor distillation teacher receives them as prompts. We reuse VAGEN interfaces for AI2-THOR Navigation [10], Sokoban, and Theory-of-Space mapping [34], training with teacher feedback rather than environment rewards. B. Result Snapshot and Provenance The core snapshot uses ﬁxed update 100 and batch 64, with 55 training-result slots. Fifteen core 4B runs, nine 9B runs, and eight additional 4B small-task online runs have local training and per-episode evaluation records; originalstudent evaluations are additional. Eleven selector-control and twelve K1/K16 endpoints are collaborator-reported 4B aggregates, accepted into the core snapshot. follow-up report adds 12 training-repetition entries, ﬁve non-reused component-control entries, and ﬁve model evaluations on an independent Navigation panel, giving 72 training-result entries in total. Their raw training logs, per-episode records, and precise subset-ID mapping have not been audited locally. We do not infer learning curves, token costs, or paired uncertainty for collaborator aggregates. SpatialGym ofﬂine K1/K16 scores retain the supplied two-decimal precision. The completed 9B extension includes original-student evaluation, K4 OPD, K4 SFT, and full-task online OPD in all three environments. Online K1/K4/K16 results now cover all three environments; SpatialGym K16 reuses the completed full 16-room baseline and is not an additional run. Deferred 9B K1/K16/full-pool adaptation and earlier 50-update, batch-16 experiments are excluded. C. Additional Training Repetitions and Independent Evaluation This section reports four additional training repetitions for each of three Navigation selectors, an independent standard Navigation panel, and the original component comparisons. All four additional repetitions are included; the original main-table endpoints and learning curves remain separate. Training repetitions. The original main-table run is reported separately, and the ﬁxed random subset in these repetitions is not identiﬁed with any of the three original random subsets. Taking the inﬁmum yields the familiar LθW1(P, Q) bound when the transport cost is ﬁnite [25], where W1 is the 1Wasserstein distance under d. This conditional statement motivates testing whether small history set approximates decisions relevant to reference distribution while permitting repeated optimization. It does not establish that the assumptions hold here, bound success, or justify any observed performance difference. Three gaps prevent treating this as guarantee for our selector. First, ordered TF-IDF similarity is not established to induce the required metric or smooth distillation loss. Second, facility-location representative weights generally differ from the actual uniform-trajectory/turn sampler; small nearest-neighbor distances alone do not bound the transport cost for these ﬁxed marginals. Third, optimization moves θ and changes its evaluation visitation distribution; ﬁxedhistory approximation says nothing by itself about cumulative errors in long-horizon environment. The lexicographic coverage-ﬁrst selector also does not inherit classical cardinality-constrained greedy guarantees [16] from this argument. 22 Independent visual-state and teacher/gradient diagnostics remain unmeasured and cannot be inferred from selector-internal similarity. Responses sampled at replay preﬁxes are not new environment states. Our evidence motivates studying coveragerepetition tradeoffs and their spatial boundary; it does not isolate causal mechanism.
